k-1.x_notes: Strengths: concrete, actual-size outline puzzles with no grid lines, so fitting pieces is a real spatial task. The star made of purple chevrons is a good challenge (I checked it: 3 chevrons, 2 ways), and every shape is correctly fillable. Clean header and footer with an id. Weaknesses: it is essentially a generic pattern-block fill-the-picture sheet (sailboat, cat, arrow, star, 'fill it again with any pieces'). There is almost nothing from the kernels: no possible vs impossible board, no fewest pieces, no finding all ways. 'Fill two different ways' and 'ask an adult to trace your pieces' put tracing work on the single adult. Only 5 short problems (about 11 fillings), so it is likely to run out before 40 minutes. This matches the organizer's complaint that K-1 is too dumbed down and ends too early.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: brings both kernels to K-1 concretely, on actual-size grid boards with picture icons of the blocks, and one shared rule stated once. P1 mixes coverable and uncoverable shapes, including an 8-triangle trapezoid that cannot be covered even though its area is even (5 up, 3 down). P2 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2/3/4 (2, 3, 4). P3 and P6 ask for all ways (2, 3 and 6 tilings; I verified the counts). P4 asks for the fewest blocks with the full set (I verified 3, 3, 4). P5 is a nice blue-block placing game with correct varied answers (first, second, first, first, second). Six substantial problems will fill the time. Weaknesses: the extra blank copies (3 hexagons for 2 ways, 4 for 3, 8 for 6) may push young children to produce duplicates. 'Say why' and finding all 6 tilings are stretches for kindergartners. The footer lacks the id.
k-1.reason: Y gives K-1 real mathematics (impossible boards, fewest pieces, finding all ways, a strategy game) at a concrete entry point and enough work for the hour. X is a pleasant but shallow shape-filling sheet that likely ends early.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: a tight, correct development of kernel 1 sized for about 40 minutes. P1 has possible and impossible boards. P2 packs blue rhombi into triangles of side 2-5 (best result: n empty), then asks why you cannot leave fewer. P3 is a well-chosen set of six boards comparing blues with chevrons. I verified the minimum empty spaces as blue/purple 0/0, 0/4, 0/0, 0/2, 1/1, 2/4, which shows that chevrons are never better and sometimes worse. Boards are actual size. Weaknesses: both impossible boards in P1 have odd area, so the first board set never forces the up/down idea. The final question 'Can you cover one purple exactly with blues?' hands over the key reason. 'Problem 2:' is restated as a second heading on page 3. The 'Fewest empty triangle spaces: Blues __ Purples __' recording line is slightly ambiguous.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: a richer, well-chosen sequence, and every answer I checked is correct. P1 includes a tileable star and an even-area trapezoid that cannot be covered (7 up, 5 down). P2 boards with holes include two up-holes (impossible), a balanced but untileable bowtie joined only at a point (a deep counterexample), and a balanced tileable board. P3 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2-5 and why the biggest needs that many. P4 generalizes to sides 10 and 100. P5 is a chevron-vs-blue table (4, 5, 4, 5 vs 2, 3, 4, 5). P6 asks children to invent a 20-triangle connected board that needs 6 greens; this is feasible. P7 asks for a rule for placing two greens on a side-2 hexagon; I checked that every up/down pair works, so the rule is clean. Weaknesses: 7 problems is more than four third graders will finish. The repeated 'explain why' prompts add some reading. The P5 chevron set is less varied than X's P3. The footer lacks the id.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are correct and usable, but Y's boards bring out the real coloring obstruction (even-area impossible boards, holes, the balanced bowtie) and add strong open problems: generalizing, inventing a board, and finding a rule. X is narrower and gives away its last insight.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: a coherent, correct development of kernel 2 on the 1-2-2 hexagon. I verified that the six cards are exactly the 6 tilings (codes RRLL, RLRL, LRRL, RLLR, LRLR, LLRR). The flip example A to B is correct, the shortest route A to F is 4 flips, the flip graph is bipartite, and the ribbon examples and rebuild ribbons are valid. The dimer-line recording trick is efficient. Weaknesses: P2 prints all six tilings right after P1 asks children to find them, which spoils the search. The ribbon work is broken into many small directed steps (P5-P9). P10 prints the intended discovery as a procedure ('Circle every neighboring RL or LR... Can you make a flip at every circled pair?'). Everything stays on one 6-tiling board, so there is little room for the strongest child, and much of the flip work happens on drawn cards rather than with blocks.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: an ambitious, open, hands-on sequence. P1 asks children to find all 6 tilings and explain why they have them all. P2 builds the flip map and asks for the farthest pair. P3 has children physically flip between given tilings on an actual-size side-2 hexagon. I verified that all six pictured tilings are valid, with minimum distances 3, 4 and 8. P4 asks for a 4-flip closed loop and whether 5 or 7 flips can work (bipartite, so no). P5 defines ribbons using an example on a different board (LRRLR, checked) and asks what a flip does to them. P6 asks for the parity proof and why E to F needs 8 flips. P7 asks for all 20 tilings of the side-2 hexagon, and P8 counts the 1-3-3 hexagon (20, which ribbons give as C(6,3)). Weaknesses: more than 40 minutes of work. P6-P7 are demanding for fourth graders and need the mathematician's support. P2 makes children redraw their P1 tilings. The flip diagrams are in light blue, and the footer lacks the id.
grades-4-5.reason: Y develops flips, distance, parity, ribbons and counting through open, block-based problems with real proofs at the end. X is correct but over-scaffolded: it hands out the tilings it just asked for and prints the flip/ribbon discovery as a procedure.

overall.reason: Y is the stronger packet in every band. Its problems are mathematically richer and correct, they stay concrete with actual-size boards, and they leave the thinking to the children. In K-1 especially it avoids the shallow, early-ending sheet the organizer has complained about. X is clean and correct but thin at K-1, narrower at 2-3, and over-directed at 4-5. Y's main fix in 15 minutes per band is trimming excess problems and adding footer ids.
